chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Writing for Ralph Marterie and losing touch with bandleaders
summary: Horace wrote four to six freelance charts for trumpeter Ralph Marterie's swinging 1950s band, then laments that Denver is off the beaten track and keeping up with bandleaders is hard.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That's good. You also have here Ralph Marterie.

Ralph Marterie, quite a trumpet player. You know, that guy was real funny. When I say funny, he was comical to me, you know. He was a little busybody, you know, but he knew what he wanted, you know, and he had a swinging band, man. And I made some things for him. I didn't do too much for Ralph. I think I made about, oh, four, six numbers, you know. And I wasn't contracted to him. I just was freelancing. I made these things, and he liked them, you know, and he had a great personnel, and some swing things -- oh, it's just coming to me now. It was a particular arrangement I made, man, and the band went over it a couple of times, man, and I would make a conductor's part so he would know what's going on, you know. Guys like Benny Goodman did the same thing, you know. They wanted to know what was happening. And he got so when the band would be shouting on the chorus, he'd scream in between there, right on those notes. He'd like that, you know. He's real versatile, and I enjoyed the guy because I liked him personally, and he was a likable sort of fellow. I haven't seen him for years, but
it was quite an experience to write for that band.
This was later, wasn't it? Was this maybe in the '50's even?

This was around the '50's because he was doing a lot of one nighters in the ballrooms and whatnot, and, of course, Ralph became quite popular, and he did some good things. Have you heard about that guy lately?
No.
I've been trying to find out where Ralph was because I wanted to get in touch with him, you know. That's the only thing, being here, with all due respect for being in Denver, sometimes --
You can lose touch.
-- you're off the beaten track.
That's true.

It's not like, you know, being in New York or being in Chicago, Detroit and the larger cities where the big bands are coming, you know, California, one of those things. They don't afford that here in Denver. So we just have to try and read, you know. Even getting the DownBeat, it doesn't give you anything, you know.

Yeah. Yeah, I really don't know where he is. There ought to be some kind of a -- like there is a musicians' guide published each year, but it doesn't deal with people in the popular jazz world. It's classical. And
it always gives the addresses of everybody and their -- who their manager and agent, that sort of thing. You can usually keep up to date.
Is it still active or not?
I think so. I can't think what the exact title is, but I've -- up to the last year or so, I believe so.
I sure would like to get one, especially if it's up to date. I know that. DownBeat used to give things in the back of the page where the musicians were playing, you know.
Yeah, but there's so many, man.
(Laughter)
Would take a --

Yes. They used to have the band-leaders, but it turned out, I think, that it had the individuals more or less in there, you know, a lot of combos, see, and it wouldn't justify what I would like to know because most of the combos that it gives, it wouldn't include the big band of the days leaders that we're talking about, you know.
